cards.name: Gravity field priority selection and blending
cards.summary: Every gravity volume carries a priority; at a position the highest priority wins, equal priorities add, and only the unit direction is handed to the player.
cards.behavior: Gravity volumes sit in one list that is kept sorted from high to low priority on every registration. A query walks the list and skips a volume when it is switched off, hidden, has no valid follower, lacks the requested type bit, or belongs to the asking object itself. Skipping the asker own volume lets a moving planet or platform ignore its own pull. The walk stops at the first volume whose priority is below the best seen. A volume with a higher priority replaces the running total. A volume with equal priority adds its vector to the total, so two overlapping fields of one tier blend by their strengths. The final vector is normalized to a unit direction, so the actor only learns which way down is. The strongest contributing volume is also returned as an info record, which is how the game reads the power class of the field the player stands in. Type bits let one level carry separate fields for ordinary pull, drop-shadow direction, magnet pull and launcher attraction. Reuse: keep a list of field objects, sort by priority, and return a normalized vector plus the dominant field.

cards.name: Inverse-square field strength with a surface offset
cards.summary: A field reports a strength of four million divided by the square of its distance from the surface, never closer than one unit, with an unlimited range unless the placement sets one.
cards.behavior: Each shape first reports a unit direction and a raw distance. The base class subtracts a per-volume offset (the planet radius for a sphere) from that distance and floors the result at one unit, so the pull never blows up on the surface. It then scales the direction by four million over the squared distance. At a distance of two thousand units the strength is exactly one, which is why the parallel and box fields use two thousand as their stand-in distance. An inverse flag negates the vector for repulsor volumes. The range test is a plain distance check against range plus the offset, and the default range is negative, which means unlimited. Note that the player does not feel this falloff: only the direction survives the normalization in the manager, and the player applies its own fixed acceleration. The strength matters for tie-breaking when equal-priority fields overlap. Reuse: keep falloff only if you blend fields; for one-field games a unit direction is enough.

constants.name: strength numerator
constants.unit: dimensionless strength times units squared, evaluated per query

constants.unit: units from the surface, evaluated per query

constants.unit: units; negative means unlimited, static default

cards.name: Spherical planet gravity toward a centre point
cards.summary: A round planet pulls toward its centre point from any direction, with the editor scale giving the radius at five hundred units per scale unit.
cards.behavior: The point field returns the unit vector from the actor to the centre and the true centre distance. The creator stores the sphere radius as the per-volume offset, equal to five hundred times the placement x scale, so strength is measured from the surface and the range test uses range plus radius. This radius is a true radius, not a diameter. A zero distance returns a zero direction instead of a divide error. Every walkable round planet and moon in the game relies on this shape, and the player pose code then keeps the character upright against the returned direction. Reuse: sphere gravity is just normalize(centre minus position); expose radius and range as designer fields and keep the surface offset for falloff.

constants.name: radius per scale unit
constants.unit: units of world length per unit of placement x scale, radius not diameter, static

cards.name: Box planet gravity by face, edge and corner regions
cards.summary: A box field splits space into face, edge and corner regions around a cuboid, so players walk across flat faces and roll around rounded edges and corners.
cards.behavior: The creator builds the box from the placement matrix with each axis scaled by five hundred times the editor scale, so these are half-extents (centre to face), and it lifts the centre by the up half-extent so the placed point sits on the base face. A query projects the position onto the three box axes and classifies it into one of twenty-seven regions: six face regions, twelve edge regions, eight corner regions and the interior. A face region pulls straight toward that face plane with a distance measured from the face and clamped at zero. An edge region pulls toward the nearest point on the edge line. A corner region pulls toward the vertex. The interior returns nothing. A six-bit mask on the volume disables individual faces, defaulting to all sixty-three, so a half-open box can leave a side without gravity. Reuse: classify by clamped local coordinates and pull toward the closest point on the box, which yields the same result for faces, edges and corners.

constants.name: half-extent per scale unit
constants.unit: units of world length per unit of placement scale, half-extent (centre to face), static

constants.name: default active face mask
constants.unit: six-bit mask, static default

cards.name: Flat plane, disk and line-segment gravity volumes
cards.summary: Parallel planes give a constant direction inside a sphere, box or cylinder, disks pull toward a round plate with edge wrap, and segments pull toward the nearest point on a line.
cards.behavior: The parallel field always returns the negative plane normal, independent of position, and reports a fixed stand-in distance (default two thousand units, designer-set base distance) so its strength equals a distant planet. Its range can be a sphere, an oriented box with optional distance growth along one axis, or a cylinder that spans from the plane up to a height and out to a radius. The disk field pulls straight toward a circular plate while the player is within the plate radius, and wraps toward the nearest rim point beyond it when edge gravity is on; it can be one-sided and can restrict itself to an angular wedge. The effective disk radius is five hundred times the largest placement scale, not the larger fallback written in the constructor. The segment field pulls toward the closest point on a line, with optional hemispherical end caps and a valid angular wedge; its default line length from the placement origin is one thousand units. A wire field samples points along a rail, defaulting to twenty interior points. Reuse: these shapes cover floating platforms, tubes, pipes and rail rides with a few distance formulas.

cards.name: Gravity direction smoothing and hard-flip transition
cards.summary: The player samples gravity at two points and keeps the sample nearest the old direction when they disagree. A turn of 72 degrees or more starts a fifteen-update transition that holds the new direction and suspends ordinary gravity.
cards.behavior: Each update the actor samples gravity at its position and at its body centre, and also a point a hundred units ahead to notice a seam. When the two main samples differ by more than about 26 degrees (dot below 0.9), the one closer to the previous direction is kept. When the new direction differs from the last one by 72 degrees or more (0.4 pi), a flip is declared and a fifteen-update window starts. During the window the new down direction is frozen. In the air, a flip of 120 degrees or more drops the old fall speed and halves the remaining velocity; a smaller flip scales the velocity to three quarters and redirects the old fall speed along the new down axis. A grounded player is flagged for re-orientation, and the body-centre offset blends back over fifteen updates. While the window runs, jump gravity is scaled to 0.3. Gravity is zero when the ground is closer than 300 units, and within 200 units the fall speed is removed and a small push of 0.1 times the normal acceleration points away from the ground, so the character floats off the new surface instead of sticking into it. The ground distance is the measured distance along gravity to the floor under the player. The body pose then rotates around the axis between old and new gravity so the model turns smoothly. Reuse: keep a short transition state on large gravity changes, freeze the direction, dampen velocity and avoid gravity near the new floor.

cards.name: Player body probe size and ceiling brake
cards.summary: The player body sensor has a radius of one hundred units centred seventy units above the feet, and a ceiling closer than one hundred sixty units slows a rising jump to sixty percent per update.
cards.behavior: The main body sensor is a sphere with radius one hundred (a radius, not a diameter). The body centre is placed along the up axis by seventy units when standing and by fifty units when crouched. While rising, the jump code measures the distance to a ceiling along the gravity axis; inside one hundred sixty units it removes the vertical speed and puts back sixty percent of it each update (ninety percent for the turn and backward flip jump kinds), so the player bonks gently instead of bouncing. Spin attacks that need headroom, such as the crouch somersault, also demand more than one hundred sixty units of clearance. Reuse: use these three numbers as a character capsule guide and a soft ceiling brake instead of a hard velocity reversal.

cards.name: Walk speed ratio with inertia blending
cards.summary: Ground speed is a zero-to-one ratio smoothed toward a stick-driven target by an exponential filter, then multiplied by thirteen units per update.
cards.behavior: The stick bucket picks one of eight target ratios from a fixed table (zero, 0.15, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, one). Each update the current ratio becomes ratio times inertia plus target times one minus inertia. Inertia is not fixed. While the stick is held it blends from 0.94 at standstill toward 0.9 at full ratio, so acceleration is quick but not instant. With the stick released it drops to 0.85, so the player stops in a few updates, and it is 0.95 when released while crouched. A turn skid and the first thirty updates after landing use their own values (0.91, 0.85 and 0.8). The ratio is multiplied by thirteen to get the displacement along the facing direction, so the top walking speed is thirteen units per update. The walk animation code multiplies per-update steps by sixty, which hints at a tick of sixty updates per second, but the update rate is not stated directly. A second table exists for the second player character; the first table is the default. Reuse: ratio = ratio * k + target * (1 - k) with k about 0.9 gives the same responsive but not instant feel.

cards.name: Heading turn blend rate while walking
cards.summary: The facing direction slerps toward the stick direction by a per-update fraction: 0.9 from standstill, 0.15 while moving and 0.04 at a slow walk.
cards.behavior: Every update the facing vector is blended on the sphere toward the desired heading by a fraction. The fraction starts at 0.9 when standing, drops to 0.15 once the speed ratio passes 0.1, and drops again to 0.04 for the lowest stick buckets, so a slow walk curves wide. On a slide or inside a spin it is 0.1, and skating halves it. After a sharp stick reversal the fraction is scaled by a square-root ramp across a fifteen-update window. When the player is not in a turning state and the ramp counter has run out, the fraction is multiplied by 0.01 so the heading holds still. While sliding down a slope the fraction is multiplied by 0.1 when the player faces the downhill direction within 45 degrees and by 0.3 otherwise. A hard reversal at speed starts a turn-around skid instead of an instant flip, which feeds the turn jump. Reuse: slerp(front, wanted, rate) per update with the rate lowered by speed and by input reversals.

cards.name: Automatic step-up over low ledges
cards.summary: Walking into a ledge lower than fifty units steps the player up without a jump.
cards.behavior: While grounded and pushing toward an obstacle, the step check looks for the top edge of the ledge. When the ledge top lies within 20 units horizontally and rises less than 50 units above the feet, a step state starts and lifts the character onto the ledge. A second branch handles a wall directly in front of a stick pushed straight at it (dot below -0.5) with the same 50-unit height limit. When the surface ahead is a gentle incline instead, the velocity is tilted to follow it. Reuse: probe from knee height, measure the ledge height and snap up when it is below a step limit.

constants.unit: units, per update, rate unverified

constants.unit: units, per update, rate unverified

cards.name: Jump launch speed and the three-step jump chain
cards.summary: A jump adds an upward impulse from a per-kind table to a forward carry of twelve and a half units times the walk ratio, and a quick re-jump after landing steps through heights 22, 26 and 36.
cards.behavior: The jump velocity is the facing direction times the current walk ratio times 12.5, plus the up axis times a height from a table indexed by jump kind. Kinds zero to two form the chain. A jump pressed within seven updates of landing, with the chaining flag set, advances the kind; otherwise the kind resets to zero. The third step needs a walk ratio of at least 0.6 or the chain falls back to the first. A fourth quick jump wraps the index to zero. The table also holds 24 for slippery or muddy ground, 32 for the turn-around and backward flips, and 15 for the long jump. A mud floor halves the up impulse. A second table for the second player character has a slightly lower third-jump height and lower gravity. The impulse is stored in a persistent jump vector that is applied each update and loses speed to gravity. Reuse: keep a chain counter reset by a timer and a speed check, and a per-kind launch table.

cards.name: Variable-height jump gravity and capped fall speed
cards.summary: Jump gravity is 1.8 units per update squared and is halved while the jump button is held or the player falls, with a terminal speed of 35 units per update, or 20 in light-gravity fields.
cards.behavior: Each update the persistent jump velocity gains gravity along the actor gravity axis, so every planet uses the same downward rule against its own direction. The base acceleration comes from a per-kind table: 1.8 for ordinary kinds and 0.95 for the long jump. That value is multiplied by 0.5 whenever the jump button is still held, the player is falling, or the jump is the third chain kind. Releasing the button while rising keeps the full value, which gives the short hop. A per-area gravity ratio multiplies it further. The fall speed along gravity is capped by a five-entry table indexed by whether the dominant gravity field has the light power class: 35 for ordinary fields and 20 for light fields; heavy fields use the ordinary value. Reuse: gravity = base * (held or falling ? 0.5 : 1), then clamp the downward speed.

cards.name: Air steering, forward decay and horizontal speed cap
cards.summary: In the air the stick adds a small steering push that fades with air time, forward carry decays by two percent per update after fifteen updates, and horizontal speed is capped at 32.
cards.behavior: Steering adds the stick direction times the walk speed (13) times three, divided by the air time in updates plus three hundred, to the jump vector each update, so control is weak at takeoff (0.13 units per update squared) and fades with air time. While falling, the stick also moves the body directly by 0.15 of the walk speed each update, which gives late-fall control. When the stick opposes the jump heading, the horizontal momentum along the old heading is reduced by ten percent times the alignment. After fifteen updates in the air, and unless the stick points backward, the horizontal speed is multiplied by 0.98 per update (0.99 after thirty for the long jump), which stops runaway carry. Backward input is amplified by up to three times at takeoff and fades to nothing after 60 updates, limited to 10 units per update. The horizontal part of the jump vector is capped at 32 units per update. Reuse: small acceleration with a 1/(t+k) fade plus a decay and a hard cap makes planet hops feel controllable.

cards.name: Long jump, backward flip and turn-around jump
cards.summary: Crouching while moving gives a low long jump of 16.5 units per update forward; crouching still gives a 32-unit backward flip; reversing at speed gives a turn jump of 32 up and 5 back.
cards.behavior: Pressing jump while crouched and moving above a 0.3 walk ratio uses the long-jump kind: forward speed 16.5, upward impulse 15, and gravity 0.95, so it is long and flat and decays slowly (0.99 per update after thirty). Pressing jump while crouched and nearly still uses the backward flip: 5 units backward and a 32 up impulse, higher than a normal jump. Pressing jump during the skid window after a stick reversal at speed uses the turn jump: 5 units opposite the old heading and a 32 up impulse, and the player faces the new direction. Those windows are ten updates of turn readiness and six updates of skid. These kinds skip the chain counter. Reuse: map them to a crouch-jump, crouch-still-jump and reverse-jump trio.

cards.name: Star spin attack, mid-air spin boost and cooldown
cards.summary: A shake triggers a spin with a 25-update hit window and a 79-update cooldown that clears on takeoff; a mid-air spin once per jump replaces the vertical speed with a 12-unit lift under very low gravity.
cards.behavior: On the ground a shake starts the spin and opens a 25-update hit window. The cooldown is 45 plus 34 updates, and any update where the player is airborne sets it back to zero, so a spin is always ready in the air. Spinning while crouched becomes a somersault that needs more than 160 units of ceiling clearance. In the air a shake first tries the mid-air spin boost, which also opens a 25-update hit window. The boost replaces the jump vector with the facing direction times the walk ratio times 5 plus 12 units per update upward, then sets gravity to 0.25 (quartered again while falling, and halved by the hold rule) and caps the horizontal speed at 6. It can fire once per jump. When the boost is not allowed, an air spin attack lasts 15 updates and zeroes the walk speed. Reuse: a gesture input, a hit window, a cooldown that resets in the air and a one-shot lift.

cards.name: Ground pound dive with acceleration limit
cards.summary: A hip drop needs at least 100 units of height, pauses two updates, then accelerates downward by up to 12 units per update squared to a speed cap of 150.
cards.behavior: The dive is refused when the player is less than 100 units above the ground, during some jump kinds while rising, or in zero gravity. The variable the code calls vertical speed is the measured distance to the ground along gravity, which also limits how far one update may move. On entry the jump vector is zeroed and a start animation plays; two more updates pass before the fall begins. Each update after that adds 12 units per update squared times a ratio that shrinks as the speed approaches 150 (0.1 plus one minus speed over 150, clamped to the range zero to one). The horizontal part is halved every update while it is above 10, so the dive goes almost straight down. The speed is hard-capped at 150. After landing, control returns when the landing animation ends, after 15 updates (45 for the spin version) when the stick is pushed, or after 5 updates when jump is pressed. The spin version also searches for targets within a 45 degree cone below, with the sweep distance capped at 500, and bends the dive toward the nearest one. Reuse: a delayed start, limited acceleration to a high cap and a heavy-landing recovery window.

cards.name: Wall cling, slide and kick-off jump
cards.summary: The player clings to a wall for 15 updates, slides at up to 14 units per update until released after 180 more, and a kick-off adds 13 along the wall normal and 30 up.
cards.behavior: A wall state keeps a timer. For the first 15 updates the player sticks with no drop. After that the drop speed eases toward 14 units per update with a 0.9 smoothing factor (a time constant of about ten updates), and the sideways movement allowance shrinks by 0.003 per update. A stick pushed into the wall behaves like a neutral stick because that branch is overwritten, so the slower 4-unit drop in the tuning table never applies. Holding the stick away from the wall pushes the timer to at least 165, so the release arrives about 30 updates later. After 195 updates in total the wall releases with a 30-unit push away from the wall (10 on slippery ground). The state also ends once the player is within 80 units of the ground. A jump press, or one buffered in the last six updates, kicks off with 13 units along the wall normal and 30 up. The kick direction is rotated slightly when a second wall follows within 15 updates. A backward kick uses 6 and 10. Reuse: a timer-based cling with a capped slide and a normal-based kick.

cards.name: Slope angle thresholds and slide acceleration
cards.summary: Slopes under 45 degrees are flat, 60 degrees starts a slide, 85 degrees counts as a wall, and a slide gains 0.01 units per update squared per degree up to a 22-unit speed cap.
cards.behavior: Floor polygons are classified by their angle to the local up axis, in degrees. The slope helpers treat 45 degrees as the boundary between flat ground and an incline. A walking player on a polygon of 60 degrees or more stops walking and starts a slide that keeps the old velocity along the slope. While the sliding flag is set, the slide velocity gains the slope angle in degrees times 0.01 per update. When the slide speed exceeds 22 (20 while braking), it is pulled toward the cap with an 0.8 to 0.2 mix. A floor steeper than 60 degrees is relabelled with a special steep-surface code after 15 updates of grace, and one steeper than 85 degrees skips the grace, so the player stops treating it as ground. While sliding, the turn fraction is multiplied by 0.1 or 0.3, so steering is weak. Reuse: use angle thresholds in degrees and an acceleration proportional to the angle for a stable slide feel.

cards.name: Swim speed model and oxygen meter
cards.summary: Swimming blends toward 7.5 units per update with 0.985 inertia, a stroke raises the speed up to 11.5, and a 3600-unit oxygen meter drains one per update after a 120-update delay.
cards.behavior: While the dive button is held, forward speed follows a filter: speed = speed * 0.985 + target * 0.015 with a target of 7.5 units per update. Without that input it decays by 0.992 per update in open water and by 0.98 at the surface. A stroke press locks input for 60 updates, runs a 40-update acceleration table and can raise the speed up to a maximum of 11.5; jet and ring modes use higher speeds. Oxygen starts at 3600. After a 120-update delay it drains one unit per update while the player is under water, it refills at 32 per update at the surface, and when empty the player takes damage once every 180 updates. Reuse: a speed filter, a stroke impulse with an input lock, and a drain meter with a refill rule.

cards.name: Enemy stomp bounce
cards.summary: Stomping an enemy launches the player up at 19 units per update, plus 4 more while jump is held, and keeps the horizontal speed.
cards.behavior: A stomp calls a forced jump that keeps the horizontal part of the old jump vector and adds an upward impulse of 19. If the jump button is held, the impulse gains 4 more, so the player can chain bounces. A special target type uses 40 as the base. When an internal stomp counter equals two, the whole launch vector is scaled by 1.2 with the button held or by 1.5 without it, before the hold bonus is added. On two named target kinds, an extra life is granted at five or eight consecutive stomps. Reuse: bounce = horizontal kept + up impulse (+ hold bonus), with a combo counter.

cards.name: Three-point health and damage knockback arc
cards.summary: The player has three health points (one in the hardest stage variant), loses one per hit, and is thrown 15 units up and 9 away with 1.0 gravity.
cards.behavior: Health starts at three and the maximum health is three; a hard challenge variant of a stage sets both to one. Each hit lowers health by one. A damage hit sets the jump vector to 15 units per update upward plus 9 units per update away from the source, then adds gravity of 1.0 per update squared each update while the damage state runs, so the arc is short and fixed. Reuse: a fixed knockback impulse and gravity define a predictable hit reaction.

cards.name: Per-area camera parameters from ground polygons and volumes
cards.summary: The game camera takes its type and parameters from the camera id painted on the polygon under the player, from camera volumes, or from built-in swim defaults, then blends over 120 updates.
cards.behavior: Each update the camera manager first checks camera volumes, then reads a camera id stored on the ground polygon (a value of 255 or more means none). The id plus the zone picks a parameter chunk; with no id the current chunk stays. Swimming and water surface states pick built-in chunks instead. A chunk carries a camera type, a look-at offset (0, 100, 0) above the target by default, a vertical field of view of 45 degrees, and a blend time of 120 updates between chunks. The built-in swim chunk uses a 170-unit look offset and the surface chunk uses distances 900 to 600. Reuse: authored per-area camera data beats one global camera for planets of different shapes.

cards.name: Follow camera orbit, auto-turn and manual 45-degree steps
cards.summary: The follow camera clamps distance and pitch toward a range, swings behind the player at a rate proportional to horizontal speed up to 15 units per update, and orbits in 45-degree steps on a button press.
cards.behavior: The orbit is polar around a look-at point. A camera farther than the maximum distance is pulled back by half of the excess each update, and one nearer than the minimum snaps to the minimum. A pitch outside its window is pulled back by half of the excess. Yaw turns toward behind-the-player at a rate in degrees per update, scaled by the horizontal speed over 15 (clamped to one) and zero while jumping. A press of the round-left or round-right button starts a 45-degree turn that converges at 0.08 radians per update, but only if a ray in that direction is free of walls. A reset press turns back behind at 0.2 radians per update. Pitch has a 75-degree look-down limit. Ray probes of 500 units from 100 units above the feet detect a wall or an incline ahead, and the pitch eases with a 0.02 spring and 0.99 damping. The values for minimum and maximum distance, pitch window and yaw rate come from per-area data, and the fallback constructor values are overridden. The fully source-visible set is the built-in water-surface camera: distances 900 and 600, a pitch window of 10 and 20 degrees, and a yaw rate of 0.15. Reuse: a polar camera with excess halving, speed-scaled auto-yaw and a stepped manual orbit.

cards.name: Camera vertical pan that lags jumps
cards.summary: The camera freezes its look-at height while the player jumps and eases its vertical position at five percent per update, using defaults of 0.3, 0.1, 300, 800 and 120.
cards.behavior: While the target is jumping, the look-at height stored at takeoff is held, so a hop does not tilt the camera. A small state machine tracks no-move, rise and fall. In every state the camera height eases toward the unpanned pose by five percent per update. The upper and lower focal fractions (0.3 and 0.1) set how far toward the top or bottom of the screen the player may travel before the look-at point is pushed along. The push ramps in over 120 updates on a rise and on a fall. The camera body then trails the look-at point by at most 300 units on a rise or 800 on a fall. After landing, the rise easing resets once half of the 160-update chase interval has passed. These defaults come from the per-area data defaults and replace the constructor values of 500 and 800. Reuse: a vertical dead zone with eased follow keeps long platforming jumps readable.

cards.name: Gravity-aware planet cameras
cards.summary: The planet orbit camera uses the negative gravity as its up axis, and the hollow-sphere camera falls toward the inner wall with 0.7 acceleration capped at 35.
cards.behavior: The median planet camera builds a frame from the player side vector, the negative gravity as up and the facing direction, and orbits in that frame, so walking around a sphere never flips the screen. It eases the pitch up to a minimum, looks at a mix of the player and a registered anchor point, and interpolates its distance between a near and a far value by the angle between the anchor up direction and the player up direction divided by pi. The hollow-sphere camera estimates the gravity centre from two samples, then moves under a pseudo gravity: its velocity gains 0.7 units per update squared along the local gravity and is capped at 35 units per update. A ray and a ball test against the map keep it off the walls, and a 0.9 to 0.1 blend smooths the distance and the up vector. The distances and angles for both cameras come from per-area data. Reuse: build the camera frame from the gravity vector rather than from world up.

cards.name: Launch star capture, shake and shoot
cards.summary: A launch star grabs the player within its 300-unit sensor, pulls them to its centre with a damped spring, fires on a shake after a 20-update wind-up, then rests for 60 updates.
cards.behavior: The star has a body sensor with a radius of 300. A shake while the star is ready captures the player at once. Without a shake the star captures only when automatic capture is enabled, the star is armed and the player is within 240 units. After a released capture the star re-arms only once the player has moved more than 350 units away. On contact the stored entry speed is capped at 40. The capture pulls the player with a spring: the velocity gains the direction to the centre times 1.5 times the distance over 120, then is multiplied by 0.8 each update, which settles at the centre. A capture without a shake ends after 40 updates once the player is within 15 units of the centre, and the player is released. A shake starts a 20-update wind-up in which the player dips 200 units below the star along its up axis and returns by the end on a fourth-power curve, and then the shoot state starts. With a rail the shoot state lasts for the flight duration (default 300 updates). Without a rail it lasts one update and releases the player at 40 units per update along the star up axis. Level data overrides both defaults. A cooldown of 60 updates follows. Reuse: a capture, pull, aim and fire state machine around a trigger gesture.

cards.name: Launch star flight path: parabola or rail
cards.summary: The flight follows a parabola when the authored path has two or fewer points, otherwise a rail curve with an eased start offset, with progress equal to the update count over the duration.
cards.behavior: A path from rail data with at most two points becomes a parabola from the star to the last rail point, with the first rail point marking the apex height. A longer rail is sampled by arc length. Progress is the update count of the shoot state divided by the duration (default 300). The player position each update is the path point at that progress, and the velocity handed back on release is the last per-update displacement, so the player carries the flight speed out. For rail paths the offset between the star and the rail head is blended out with an ease-out curve over the first half of the flight. The facing turns toward the travel direction by 0.4 per update. Between the start of the landing animation and 20 updates before the end, the player rotates a half turn around the side axis, and the fall animation starts 20 updates before the end. Reuse: drive the player along a precomputed curve by normalized time and hand the last displacement back on release.
